prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of GLP-1 physiology and the active incretin peptide that enabled GLP-1-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six openings placed B003 first, but I do not treat that as merit in itself. The merit is that the arc runs from gut-hormone physiology (Holst on secretion and action of GLP-1, Drucker on receptor biology and the therapeutic concept, Mojsov on the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide) to a clinical effect that is large, durable and confirmed in independent outcome trials. It is also timely, since the biology reaches beyond metabolism into appetite-regulating brain circuits. A single achievement with a three-person discovery core is the cleanest configuration on the shortlist, and I think a discovery-anchored prize is better supported than one anchored on drug development.
statement.case_against: The attribution is the weakest point. The early GLP-1 peptide-identification credit (Mojsov versus the Habener group, who are not on the shortlist) is contested, and none of us can settle it from the supplied names. Omitting Knudsen leaves out the person most responsible for liraglutide and semaglutide. If the committee will not accept that a prize can honour physiology without the drug developers, the configuration is vulnerable. I have not independently verified the priority claims, and a prize that bakes in a disputed attribution would be hard to defend.

responses.point: Svenningsson puts Knudsen in the trio with Drucker and Holst and drops Mojsov. He argues that Mojsov's weight is contested and that the medicinal chemistry behind the approved drugs is part of the achievement.
responses.response: This is the real disagreement in the room, and I do not fully agree. The shortlist entry covers both GLP-1 physiology and the development of incretin therapies, so Knudsen has a legitimate claim. But her contribution is medicinal chemistry for long-acting analogues, which is development built on the discovery. Mojsov's identification of the biologically active form is the step that made any such drug rational. A contested priority claim argues for care in the citation wording, not for removing her. I would reconsider only if the committee wants an explicit physiology-plus-drug-development prize, which the three-person cap makes awkward.

responses.point: Perlmann ranks B043 (Walter and Mori) second and values its clean, original conceptual shift in cell biology. He also notes that Knudsen's work is drug development and may suit a different recognition.
responses.response: I agree with him on Knudsen, and I take B043 seriously as the best purely basic-science candidate here. I rank it behind B003 because its human clinical consequence is still developing, whereas GLP-1 has both mechanism and demonstrated outcome. My reservation about B043 is the PERK and ATF6 arms: Ron and others are outside the credited names, so a Walter and Mori prize may cover only part of the pathway. I would want that settled before supporting it over a mature therapeutic discovery.

responses.point: Sandberg ranks cGAS-STING third and Hall with Schreiber for TOR fourth, omitting Sabatini. He also flags the Habener and Mojsov credit dispute as unresolved from the supplied text.
responses.response: I share his caution on the Habener and Mojsov credit, which I think is the main open question on B003. On cGAS-STING, I rank it seventh because the mechanism is secure but the clinical consequence is not yet established, so recognition looks somewhat early next to B003. On TOR, the biology is foundational, but the allocation among Hall, Schreiber, Sabatini and others is unresolved and the therapeutic payoff is partial. My concern there is about credit and consequence, not only the reputational issue he cites.

responses.point: Linnarsson ranks B040 (Krainer and Bennett) third and calls it a clean, well-matched pair that turned a fatal childhood disease into a treatable one. He ranks optogenetics sixth, with a methods-versus-therapy caveat.
responses.response: B040 has a clean pair and an unambiguous clinical effect, and I agree with him on that. I place it below the top tier because it is a therapeutic application of splicing biology with a shorter follow-up than the other candidates. On optogenetics I disagree with the lower rank: it is a method, but it changed how causal circuit questions are asked, which is why I ranked it second. I should declare that this is close to my field and not let that raise it further, and the six-name attribution problem is real.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's contribution to the active GLP-1 peptide can be credited without ignoring the Habener group, who are outside the supplied names.
Whether the committee accepts discovery-only credit for B003 or insists on including drug development (Knudsen).
For B036, whether to honour the channelrhodopsin discovery (Nagel, Hegemann, Bamberg) or the neuronal implementation (Deisseroth, Boyden) is unresolved under a three-person cap.
statement.conflict_note: I work in motor-circuit neuroscience, so the optogenetics candidate (B036) is in a field close to mine and I have tried to apply the common criteria rather than field familiarity. No specific personal or institutional conflict with the shortlisted candidates is apparent from my provided profile. I co-authored a 2019 review with Sten Grillner and a 2009 paper with Thomas Perlmann, but neither is a candidate and I do not regard these as recusal grounds.
